chapters.title: Measure rate and infer an experimental law
chapters.formula: rate = k[A]²[B]; order = 3; k = 2.0 M⁻² s⁻¹
points: For 2A → B, reaction rate is half the disappearance rate of A.
Doubling A at fixed B quadruples rate: order in A is 2.
Doubling B at fixed A doubles rate: order in B is 1.
chapters.script: Welcome to Chemical Kinetics. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. Kinetics asks how quickly a reaction proceeds. Equilibrium asks about its preferred composition. A thermodynamically favourable reaction can still be slow. Average rate describes a finite interval; instantaneous rate is the local slope of the concentration time curve. For two A forming B at constant volume, A disappears twice as quickly as B forms. Divide the disappearance rate of A by its coefficient two to obtain the normalized reaction rate. If A disappears at zero point zero four zero molar per second, the reaction rate is zero point zero two zero molar per second. Read whether the question asks for a species rate or the normalized rate. Now determine a rate law from experiments. Our first experiment uses A and B concentrations each zero point one zero molar and gives rate zero point zero zero two zero molar per second. In the second, only A doubles and the rate quadruples. The exponent of A is therefore two. In the third, only B doubles and the rate doubles. Its exponent is one. The law is k times A squared times B, with total order three. Do not copy those exponents from an overall chemical equation; they are experimental results. Substitute the first row to find k. Divide zero point zero zero two zero by zero point one squared times zero point one. The result is two point zero, with units molar to the minus two per second. At unchanged temperature and conditions, tripling A and halving B changes rate by nine times one half, or four point five. Each concentration ratio gets its own exponent. Overall order three does not mean every mixed change gets cubed.

chapters.title: Distinguish order and molecularity; solve zero order
points: Order comes from the measured rate law; molecularity refers to an elementary step.
Depletion at 40.0 min: do not extrapolate to negative concentration.
chapters.script: Order and molecularity answer different questions. Total order is the sum of exponents in an empirical rate law. It may be zero or fractional. Molecularity counts reacting entities in a single elementary step and is a positive integer. Do not assign molecularity to an arbitrary multistep overall equation. If rate uses concentration per time and total order is r, the units of k are concentration to the power one minus r, divided by time. A first order k has inverse time units. A zero order k has concentration per time units. For an order of one half, k has concentration to the one half per time. Units are a useful check, not a substitute for reading the experiment. For zero order disappearance, the concentration decreases by a fixed amount per unit time while the model holds. Integrating gives concentration at time t equals initial concentration minus k times t. A plot of concentration against time is straight with slope minus k. Take initial concentration zero point zero eight zero zero molar and k zero point zero zero two zero zero molar per minute. After fifteen minutes the loss is zero point zero three zero zero molar, leaving zero point zero five zero zero. Setting concentration to zero gives depletion time forty minutes. Extrapolating beyond that would predict a negative concentration and is physically invalid. The zero order half life is initial concentration divided by two k. Here it is twenty minutes. Doubling the initial concentration doubles that half life at the same k. A zero order description can apply over a limited range, such as a saturated catalyst surface. State its valid range rather than assuming that the same straight line governs every possible concentration.

chapters.title: First order removes equal fractions
points: With t½=10.0 min, after 30.0 min only 12.5% remains.
90% completion leaves 10%: t=ln(10)/k=33.2 min.
75% to 93.75% consumption requires two additional half-lives.
chapters.script: For first order disappearance, the rate is proportional to the amount still present. Equal time intervals remove equal fractions rather than equal amounts. The integrated law is the natural logarithm of initial concentration divided by remaining concentration equals k times t. The ratio inside the logarithm is dimensionless. The half life is natural log two divided by k and is independent of the starting concentration in this model. Suppose the half life is ten minutes. Thirty minutes is three half lives, so the fraction remaining is one half cubed, or one eighth. That is twelve point five percent remaining, not twelve point five percent consumed. For ninety percent completion, ten percent remains. Calculate k as natural log two divided by ten, about zero point zero six nine three one per minute. The required time is natural log ten divided by k, about thirty three point two minutes. Never replace percent remaining by percent consumed inside the logarithm. Here is another check. A reactant is seventy five percent consumed in twenty minutes. One quarter remains, so two half lives have elapsed and each half life is ten minutes. To reach ninety three point seven five percent consumption, one sixteenth must remain. That is four half lives in total, or forty minutes. The additional time after the first observation is twenty minutes. A plot of natural log concentration against time is straight with slope minus k, using a consistent concentration reference. Finally, keep the time unit consistent. A k value of zero point one two zero per minute equals zero point zero zero two zero zero per second. Multiplying an inverse minute constant by a time in seconds without conversion gives the wrong decay.

chapters.title: Convert total gas pressure into reactant pressure
chapters.formula: A → B + C: pA = 2P0 − Ptotal; k = ln(100/50)/10
points: Assume ideal gases, constant temperature and volume, and initially pure A.
P0=100 kPa; Ptotal=150 kPa → pA=50 kPa.
First-order k=0.0693 min⁻¹; total pressure is not remaining A.
chapters.script: Pressure measurements can reveal a rate constant, but only after stoichiometry connects pressure to the reactant. Assume initially pure ideal gas A decomposes to one B plus one C. Temperature and volume stay constant, and no other gases or reactions are present. Let the reacted fraction be f. Starting with n zero moles, the remaining A is n zero times one minus f. The amounts of B and C are each n zero f. Total moles are therefore n zero times one plus f. At fixed temperature and volume, total pressure divided by initial pressure equals one plus f. If the initial pressure is one hundred kilopascals and the total pressure after ten minutes is one hundred fifty, f is one half. Remaining A has partial pressure fifty kilopascals. Equivalently, A's partial pressure is twice the initial pressure minus the current total pressure. Use that partial pressure in the first order disappearance law, because it is proportional to A concentration under the stated conditions. k equals natural log of one hundred divided by fifty, all divided by ten minutes. The answer is about zero point zero six nine three per minute. Total pressure rises because one reactant molecule produces two product molecules, while the amount of A falls. Directly inserting total pressure into a disappearance formula would give the wrong sign. Check the limiting pressures. At the beginning, total pressure is one hundred. At complete conversion it approaches two hundred in this model. If the reaction stoichiometry, initial mixture, temperature or volume changes, derive a new pressure relation. Do not memorize twice initial minus total as a universal gas kinetics formula. The reliable method is a mole balance followed by the ideal gas relation.

chapters.title: Temperature, collisions and catalysts
points: If k doubles from 300 to 310 K, Ea≈53.6 kJ/mol for constant A.
In ln k versus 1/T, slope = −Ea/R.
A catalyst changes the pathway, not equilibrium constant at fixed temperature.
chapters.script: The Arrhenius model writes k as A times the exponential of minus activation energy divided by R T. Use temperature in kelvin and match the energy units of activation energy and R. If A is approximately constant and activation energy is positive, higher temperature increases k. Comparing two temperatures gives natural log of k two over k one equals activation energy over R, multiplied by one over T one minus one over T two. Suppose k doubles between three hundred and three hundred ten kelvin. Use R equal to eight point three one four joules per mole kelvin. Activation energy is R times natural log two, divided by one over three hundred minus one over three hundred ten. The result is about fifty three thousand six hundred joules per mole, or fifty three point six kilojoules per mole. The sign is positive, as expected. A plot of natural log k against inverse temperature has slope minus activation energy over R. There is no universal rule that every ten degree rise doubles every reaction rate. In elementary collision theory for gaseous bimolecular reactions, encounters need sufficient energy and suitable orientation. Counting all collisions as successful would overestimate the reaction rate. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower effective activation barrier and speeds the approach to equilibrium. At unchanged temperature it does not change the equilibrium constant or the reaction enthalpy. It may participate in intermediate steps without being consumed in the net reaction. Finish each kinetics problem by identifying the rate definition, selecting the order and model, converting units, and checking physical limits. Use the twelve original practice questions and the seven worked examples in the notes. This recording covers the core foundation of Unit eight; broader experimental datasets and mechanism practice remain useful. The questions are original practice, not official past papers.

chapters.title: Normalize rates using coefficients
chapters.script: A reaction rate and a species disappearance rate are not always the same number. For the balanced decomposition of two moles of dinitrogen pentoxide into four moles of nitrogen dioxide and one mole of oxygen, divide each concentration slope by its stoichiometric coefficient. Suppose dinitrogen pentoxide disappears at zero point zero zero four zero moles per litre per second at constant volume. The normalized forward reaction rate is half that value, zero point zero zero two zero. Nitrogen dioxide appears four times as fast as the normalized rate, giving zero point zero zero eight zero. Oxygen appears at zero point zero zero two zero. All three statements describe the same reaction progress. The negative sign in a disappearance derivative makes the forward rate positive; it does not mean the concentration is negative. These coefficient relationships follow from stoichiometry, while experimental concentration exponents in a rate law are a different matter. If volume changes substantially, account for that change before identifying a concentration derivative with a simple molar production rate. Read exactly which species and which definition the question requests.

chapters.title: Pseudo-first-order conditions
chapters.script: A reaction can appear first order when one concentration remains nearly constant. Consider an experimentally established disappearance law for A equal to k times A concentration times B concentration. If B is present in very large excess, consuming A changes B only slightly over the measurement interval. Combine k and the effectively constant B concentration into an observed first order constant. With k equal to zero point zero two zero litres per mole per second and B concentration zero point five zero moles per litre, the observed constant is zero point zero one zero per second. The predicted half life of A is about sixty nine point three seconds. The original constant still has second order units, while the observed constant has inverse time units. Doubling the maintained B concentration doubles the observed constant and halves that half life within the model. This does not turn the underlying overall order into a universal first order law. If B is depleted significantly, the approximation fails. In ester hydrolysis examples, solvent and catalyst conditions must also be controlled rather than silently absorbed into an unexplained constant.

chapters.title: Choose a graph that tests the model
chapters.formula: Zero order: [A] versus t; first order: ln([A]/[A]₀) versus t
chapters.script: Graph selection can distinguish an amount removed from a fraction removed. Under zero order disappearance, concentration itself decreases linearly with time and the slope is minus the zero order constant. For first order disappearance, the natural logarithm of the remaining concentration divided by its initial value is linear, with slope minus the first order constant. Using the ratio keeps the logarithm dimensionless. Equal successive half lives support a first order model; a half life proportional to starting concentration supports zero order over its applicable range. Suppose a first order logarithmic plot has slope minus zero point zero three zero per minute. The constant is positive zero point zero three zero per minute and half life is about twenty three point one minutes. A straight concentration plot with slope minus zero point zero zero three zero moles per litre per minute instead has a zero order constant with concentration per time units. Do not compare those numerical slopes as if their units matched. A good fit over a narrow interval is evidence for a model, not proof of an elementary mechanism.

chapters.title: Completion percentages and half-lives
chapters.script: A completion percentage must be converted into the fraction still present. For a first order reactant with a ten minute half life, seventy five percent completion leaves one quarter, requiring two half lives or twenty minutes. Eighty seven point five percent completion leaves one eighth, requiring thirty minutes. Ninety nine point nine percent completion leaves one thousandth, not nine hundred ninety nine thousandths. Its time is the natural logarithm of one thousand divided by the constant. Since the constant is the natural logarithm of two divided by ten minutes, the time is about ninety nine point seven minutes. Thus nearly ten half lives are needed, even though the final amount is very small. Exact one hundred percent completion would require the logarithm of an infinite concentration ratio in this ideal continuous model; it has no finite predicted time. Real measurements have detection limits and the model may cease to apply at very low concentrations. For the same first order law, the ratio of ninety percent completion time to half life is the natural logarithm of ten divided by the natural logarithm of two.

chapters.title: Catalyst barriers and reaction energy
chapters.formula: Ea,forward − Ea,reverse = ΔH for this energy profile
chapters.script: An energy profile separates a barrier from the energy difference between products and reactants. In an illustrative single barrier enthalpy diagram, set reactants at zero and products at minus thirty kilojoules per mole. An uncatalysed peak at plus eighty gives a forward barrier of eighty and a reverse barrier of one hundred ten. The reverse barrier is measured upward from the lower product level, not from zero. If an alternative catalytic path has a peak at plus sixty with the same endpoints, its forward and reverse barriers are sixty and ninety. Both decrease, while the reaction enthalpy remains minus thirty. A real catalytic mechanism can contain several intermediates and barriers; this simple diagram illustrates the bookkeeping. The catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature, although it can change how quickly equilibrium is approached. Barrier differences alone do not guarantee a numerical rate ratio unless the relevant prefactors and kinetic model are also specified. Keep potential energy sketches, thermodynamic direction and experimentally measured rates distinct.

chapters.title: Read the logarithm before using the Arrhenius slope
chapters.script: An Arrhenius graph is useful only after identifying both axes and the logarithm convention. For a fixed mechanism with an approximately constant pre exponential factor, the natural logarithm of the rate constant equals the natural logarithm of that factor minus activation energy divided by R T. A graph of natural logarithm k against reciprocal absolute temperature therefore has slope minus activation energy divided by R. Suppose its measured slope is minus six thousand kelvin. Multiplying the positive magnitude by R, eight point three one four joules per mole kelvin, gives activation energy forty nine point eight eight four kilojoules per mole. If the vertical axis instead uses base ten logarithm k, the slope contains an additional factor two point three zero three in the denominator. Applying the natural logarithm formula to that graph would give the wrong energy. Also inspect horizontal scaling: a graph against one thousand divided by temperature does not have the same numerical slope as one against reciprocal temperature. A straight segment supports a useful model over its measured range; it does not prove the mechanism and pre exponential factor remain unchanged at every temperature.

log₁₀ k vs 1/T · Slope = −Ea/(2.303R) · Different slope convention

chapters.title: Infer fractional orders from controlled initial rates
chapters.script: Experimental reaction order need not be an integer and need not equal a balanced equation coefficient. Consider three initial rate measurements at the same temperature and with the same preparation conditions. In the first experiment, A and B concentrations are both zero point one zero zero molar, and the initial rate is zero point zero zero two zero molar per second. In the second, A is increased fourfold while B stays fixed, and the rate doubles. Thus four raised to the order in A equals two, giving order one half. In the third experiment, return A to its original value and triple B. If the initial rate triples, the order in B is one. The overall order is three halves. Dividing rate by the square root of A concentration and by B concentration gives a rate constant with units molarity to the negative one half per second. Fractional order describes an observed rate law; molecularity is a count for an elementary event and is not assigned a fractional value. Use initial rates so changing composition during a run does not obscure the controlled comparison.

A fixed; B ×3 · Initial rate ×3 · Order in B = 1

chapters.title: Separate dilution from chemical conversion
chapters.formula: Instant dilution changes concentration, not the surviving amount
chapters.script: A sudden concentration decrease is not always evidence that reactant has been consumed. Take a first order reaction in a closed well mixed liquid, with rate constant zero point zero six nine three one per minute. At the selected instant there are zero point one zero zero moles of reactant in one litre. Add inert solvent rapidly so the volume becomes two litres, with no reaction during the idealized mixing step. The amount remains zero point one zero zero moles, but concentration falls from zero point one zero zero to zero point zero five zero zero molar. After mixing, assume the temperature, medium effects and first order rate constant remain unchanged. Ten minutes later, about half the amount remains: zero point zero five zero zero moles in two litres, or zero point zero two five zero zero molar. Using the original concentration as though no dilution occurred would mistake mixing for additional reaction. Real dilution may alter a rate constant through solvent or ionic effects; constancy is an assumption here. Keep separate records of amount, volume and elapsed reaction time before choosing an integrated concentration ratio.

chapters.title: Supporting application: competing first-order pathways
chapters.formula: A → B and A → C: ktotal = kB + kC
chapters.script: As a supporting rate law application, suppose one reactant can form either B or C through independent irreversible first order pathways. Let the rate constants be zero point zero two zero and zero point zero three zero per minute, respectively. Assume both stay constant, the products do not react further, and the initial products are absent. Reactant disappears through both channels, so its total first order loss constant is zero point zero five zero per minute. Its half life is the natural logarithm of two divided by that total, about thirteen point eight six minutes. Product formation rates have ratio two to three at every instant, because both contain the same current reactant concentration. Integrating gives forty percent of reacted A as B and sixty percent as C in this ideal model. When half of an initial one mole has reacted, B amount is zero point two zero mole and C amount zero point three zero mole. These are fractions of reacted material, not fractions of the remaining reactant. Reversible steps, product loss or different orders require another model; adding constants blindly is not a general rule for reaction networks.

chapters.title: Subtract the baseline before fitting first order
chapters.script: A measured signal can track concentration without being equal to concentration. Suppose a first order disappearance is monitored by a calibrated signal S equal to a constant baseline plus a constant factor times reactant concentration. The baseline is zero point one zero zero, the initial signal zero point nine zero zero, and the signal after ten minutes zero point five zero zero. Subtracting the baseline gives an initial excess zero point eight zero zero and a later excess zero point four zero zero. The concentration fraction remaining is one half, so the rate constant is natural logarithm two divided by ten, or zero point zero six nine three one per minute. Using the raw ratio zero point five divided by zero point nine would be incorrect. This analysis assumes a linear calibration, a constant response factor and an endpoint signal that represents complete reactant disappearance. Other absorbing species or instrumental drift require their own model. A fitted first order constant describes the observed kinetic law, not necessarily an elementary step.

chapters.title: Add first-order exposure across temperature stages
chapters.script: A reaction experiencing two temperature stages cannot generally use a simple arithmetic average of rate constants. Consider a first order disappearance in a fixed volume with no material added or removed. During the first ten minutes, the supplied rate constant is natural logarithm two divided by ten per minute. Half of the initial reactant remains. During the next five minutes at a different temperature, the rate constant is natural logarithm two divided by five per minute. This stage removes half of what remains, leaving one quarter of the initial amount overall. Each segment contributes its own dimensionless exposure, k times time. The total exposure is two natural logarithms of two. An effective constant for the whole fifteen minutes is this sum divided by fifteen, about zero point zero nine two four two per minute. It is a time weighted summary for this schedule, not the rate constant at an average temperature. This model treats temperature changes as instantaneous and ignores conversion during the transitions. Finite heating ramps instead require an integral of the temperature dependent constant over time.

chapters.title: A smaller barrier does not alone fix a rate ratio
chapters.script: Comparing activation energies alone is insufficient when Arrhenius prefactors differ. Use two supplied first order processes at three hundred kelvin. Process X has a prefactor one tenth that of process Y, while its activation energy is lower by R T times natural logarithm ten at this temperature. The energy advantage is about five point seven four kilojoules per mole using R equal to eight point three one four joules per mole kelvin. In the ratio of Arrhenius constants, the prefactor contributes zero point one and the exponential contributes ten. Their product is one, so the two rate constants are equal at three hundred kelvin. This equality need not hold at another temperature if the activation energies and prefactors remain fixed. A prefactor has the units of its own rate constant; numerical comparisons require compatible rate-law definitions and units. The example does not infer an elementary mechanism or a universal compensation rule. Separate the energy-dependent exponential from collision frequency and orientation contributions before turning a barrier comparison into a numerical rate prediction.

chapters.title: Supporting extension: an intermediate can rise and fall
chapters.formula: For A→B→C with equal first-order k: [B]/[A]₀=kt exp(−kt)
chapters.script: A sequential reaction can make an intermediate accumulate and then disappear. This is a supporting application of first order laws, not an additional required integrated-order formula. Consider the ideal sequence A forming B, followed by B forming C, with both irreversible steps having the same constant k in a fixed volume. Initially only A is present, and each step has one to one stoichiometry. Use the supplied result: the fraction present as B is k t times exponential minus k t. At time one divided by k, that fraction reaches its maximum, one divided by e, about zero point three six eight. At that instant A also has fraction one divided by e, and C has fraction one minus two divided by e, about zero point two six four. The three fractions sum to one. If k is zero point one zero zero per minute, the intermediate peaks at ten minutes. Unequal rate constants, reverse reactions or material removal change these expressions. A falling intermediate concentration does not mean its formation has stopped; it means its consumption rate exceeds its formation rate.

chapters.title: A clock time measures a specified product threshold
chapters.formula: Mean formation rate = cumulative product threshold / elapsed time
chapters.script: A clock measurement records the time needed to reach a specified chemical threshold. It does not directly measure a rate constant. Suppose a calibrated iodine clock signals after a cumulative iodine production of zero point zero zero zero two zero zero mole per litre of final mixture. This is iodine produced over the interval, not necessarily free iodine accumulated, because a fast auxiliary reaction can consume iodine until its scavenger is exhausted. Reaching that same threshold in twenty seconds gives average iodine formation rate one point zero zero times ten to the negative five mole per litre per second. Forty seconds gives half that rate. Comparing reciprocal times is valid only when the threshold and volume convention match. If conversion is small enough that reactant concentrations barely change, these averages may approximate initial rates. A large threshold, changing scavenger amount, mixing delay or a different detection criterion can invalidate that shortcut. In the thiosulfate clock model, two thiosulfates consume one iodine, so the cumulative iodine threshold is half the initial thiosulfate concentration in the final mixture. This is interpretation of supplied measurements, not a preparation procedure.

chapters.title: A tangent rate differs from a finite-interval average
chapters.script: Average and instantaneous rates answer different questions about the same concentration curve. Consider a supplied first order disappearance at fixed volume with initial concentration zero point one zero zero molar and rate constant zero point one zero zero per minute. After ten minutes, concentration is zero point one times exponential minus one, about zero point zero three six eight molar. The mean disappearance rate over those ten minutes is the lost concentration divided by ten, about zero point zero zero six three two molar per minute. At the midpoint, five minutes, the instantaneous rate is instead k times the concentration at that instant, about zero point zero zero six zero seven molar per minute. A secant slope over an interval and a tangent slope at one time need not agree, even if that time is the interval midpoint. For this decaying exponential the rate falls continuously as reactant disappears. Shortening an interval around a chosen instant makes its mean approach the tangent value, subject to measurement uncertainty. A straight line concentration trace would be a different case in which interval and tangent slopes are equal.

chapters.title: Supporting balance: changing volume also changes concentration
chapters.script: Concentration can fall because a substance reacts and because its occupied volume increases. As a supporting material balance, consider a uniform closed reacting system whose boundary can move, with no inflow or outflow of A. Write its amount as concentration times volume. Differentiating that product gives amount change equal to volume times concentration change plus concentration times volume change. Define the positive chemical disappearance rate per current volume as r. Then the concentration derivative is negative r minus concentration divided by volume times the volume derivative. At a specified instant let volume be one litre, A concentration zero point one zero zero molar, chemical disappearance rate zero point zero zero two zero zero molar per second and expansion rate zero point zero one zero zero litre per second. The expansion contributes an additional concentration decrease of zero point zero zero one zero zero molar per second. The observed concentration slope is therefore negative zero point zero zero three zero zero, while chemical amount loss is only zero point zero zero two zero zero mole per second. This distinction extends the constant volume rate definition; it is not an additional required integrated-order law.

chapters.title: Supporting model: reversible first-order relaxation
chapters.formula: A ⇌ B: krelax = kf + kr; [B]eq/[A]eq = kf/kr
chapters.script: A reversible first order model approaches an equilibrium plateau rather than consuming all reactant. Consider a fixed volume closed system with one to one conversion between A and B. Let forward and reverse constants be zero point one zero zero and zero point zero five zero zero per minute, and let their conserved total concentration be zero point three zero zero molar. Equal opposing rates at equilibrium give B to A concentration ratio two. The equilibrium concentrations are therefore zero point two zero zero molar B and zero point one zero zero molar A. The supplied relaxation result says displacement from equilibrium decays with the sum of the two constants, zero point one five zero per minute. Its half time is natural logarithm two divided by that sum, about four point six two minutes. Starting with only A, after one such half time B is zero point one zero zero molar and A is zero point two zero zero. This halves the distance to equilibrium, not the initial A concentration. It is a supporting kinetic model, not a universal formula for every reversible mechanism. The ratio of these two constants describes equilibrium only for the stated compatible rate laws.

chapters.title: A ten-kelvin rate multiplier depends on the starting temperature
chapters.script: The statement that a reaction doubles its rate constant for every ten degree rise is an approximate shortcut, not a universal Arrhenius identity. Suppose the rate constant doubles between three hundred and three hundred ten kelvin. Assume one unchanged mechanism, a temperature independent activation energy and a constant pre exponential factor across the small range. The logarithm of the rate constant ratio equals activation energy over the gas constant times the difference of reciprocal absolute temperatures. Using the gas constant eight point three one four gives an activation energy about fifty three point six kilojoules per mole. For the next interval, three hundred ten to three hundred twenty kelvin, the reciprocal temperature difference is smaller. Divide that new difference by the first difference to obtain three hundred over three hundred twenty. The next multiplier is therefore two raised to that ratio, approximately one point nine one five, rather than exactly two. This calculation compares rate constants. Actual reaction rates also depend on concentrations through the experimental rate law. Use kelvin throughout, preserve the sign, and do not extrapolate a fitted activation energy across a mechanism change.
points: k310/k300=2; constant Ea and prefactor · Ea=R ln2/(1/300−1/310) · Ea≈53.6 kJ/mol

chapters.title: An inert gas changes the total-pressure bookkeeping
chapters.formula: A→2B; pA=2pA,0+pI−Ptotal at fixed T,V; k=ln(pA,0/pA)/t for first order
chapters.script: A total pressure measurement contains every gas, including an inert gas that does not react. Consider a closed rigid vessel at constant temperature. Initially reactant A has partial pressure eighty kilopascals and an inert gas has forty kilopascals. There is initially no product. The only reaction is one A forming two B. Let the pressure equivalent of the reacted amount be x. Reactant pressure becomes eighty minus x, product pressure becomes twice x, and inert pressure stays forty. Total pressure is therefore one hundred twenty plus x. At a measured total pressure of one hundred sixty kilopascals, x is forty, leaving reactant pressure forty and product pressure eighty. If disappearance is first order and this reading occurs after one hundred seconds, the rate constant is the natural logarithm of two divided by one hundred, about zero point zero zero six nine three per second. The correct reconstruction uses twice the initial reactant partial pressure plus inert pressure minus total pressure. Twice the initial total pressure minus the current total pressure would give the wrong result. These equations require ideal gases, fixed temperature and volume, and the supplied single reaction.

chapters.title: Supporting inference: a measured fraction gives a range of rate constants
chapters.script: A calculated rate constant inherits the uncertainty of the measurement used to obtain it. Consider a supporting inference exercise under an already accepted irreversible first order model, at fixed temperature and volume. After one hundred seconds, a calibrated experiment bounds the fraction remaining between zero point four eight and zero point five two. Treat these as supplied bounds, not as a statistical confidence interval, and neglect timing error. The rate constant equals negative natural logarithm of the fraction divided by time. Because the logarithm increases with its argument, the larger remaining fraction gives the smaller disappearance constant. The lower constant is negative logarithm of zero point five two divided by one hundred, about zero point zero zero six five three nine per second. The upper constant uses zero point four eight, about zero point zero zero seven three four zero per second. Half life is natural logarithm of two divided by the constant, so its bounds run in the opposite order: approximately ninety four point four to one hundred six seconds. A midpoint measurement would suggest one hundred seconds, but cannot erase the supplied interval. One bounded reading also does not establish the reaction order by itself.

chapters.title: Supporting mechanism: cancel species before deriving an apparent law
chapters.formula: Fast A+B⇌I; slow I+C→P+B; net A+C→P; v=k₂Kc[A][B][C] under pre-equilibrium
chapters.script: A proposed mechanism can contain species absent from the net reaction, yet those species can affect its rate. Use a hypothetical supporting mechanism with a fast reversible association of A and B to form intermediate I, followed by a slow elementary reaction of I with C to give P and regenerate B. Adding the forward steps cancels I and B, leaving A plus C forming P. Intermediate I is produced first and consumed later. Catalyst B is consumed first and regenerated later. If the fast first step remains close to equilibrium while the slow step consumes I, its concentration is the concentration equilibrium constant times free A times free B. The slow elementary step has rate constant k two times I times C. Substitution gives k two times the equilibrium constant times free A, free B and C: an apparent third order law in this specified regime. The two elementary forward steps are each bimolecular; there is no three body elementary collision implied by the overall third order law. Free B must not automatically be replaced by total catalyst when appreciable B is bound in I. This conditional derivation illustrates reasoning, not proof that a real reaction follows this mechanism.
points: Fast A+B⇌I; slow I+C→P+B · Cancel I and B in the forward sum · Net A+C→P; B is regenerated

Free [B], not automatically total B · Both forward elementary steps bimolecular · Apparent order 3 is not molecularity 3

quiz.question: For 2A -> B, A disappears at 0.040 M/s. The normalized reaction rate is:
quiz.explanation: Divide the reactant disappearance rate by its stoichiometric coefficient two.

quiz.question: The units of a first-order k are:
quiz.explanation: A first-order rate constant has inverse-time units because rate is k times concentration.

quiz.question: Molecularity is defined for:
quiz.explanation: It counts the reacting entities involved in one elementary step, not a multistep overall equation.

quiz.question: After two first-order half-lives, the fraction remaining is:
quiz.explanation: Each half-life halves what remains, so two successive halvings give one quarter.

quiz.question: Doubling [A]_0 in a zero-order disappearance model changes its half-life by:
quiz.explanation: The zero-order half-life is [A]_0/(2k), proportional to the starting concentration.

quiz.question: A plot of ln k against 1/T in the simple Arrhenius model has slope:
quiz.explanation: Taking natural logs gives ln k = ln A - (E_a/R)(1/T), identifying the negative slope.

quiz.question: For pure A -> B + C at constant temperature and volume, P0 = 100 kPa and current total pressure is 150 kPa. A partial pressure is:
quiz.explanation: For these assumptions p_A = 2P0-P_total = 50 kPa. Total pressure is not the remaining reactant partial pressure.

quiz.question: A zero-order model predicts [A] = -0.010 M after a long time. The correct interpretation is:
options: The linear model has been extrapolated beyond its valid range
quiz.explanation: The depletion boundary must be respected; the model cannot create a physically negative amount.

quiz.question: For rate = k[A]^2[B], tripling A and halving B changes rate by a factor of:
quiz.explanation: Each concentration ratio gets its own exponent: 3 squared times one half is 4.5.

quiz.question: For a first-order reaction, 75 percent consumption corresponds to:
quiz.explanation: A quarter remains, so two successive halvings have occurred. Percentage consumed must be converted to fraction remaining.

quiz.question: A first-order k of 0.120 min^-1 equals:
quiz.explanation: One minute is sixty seconds, so divide the inverse-minute value by sixty.

quiz.question: For rate = k[A]^(1/2), with rate in M/s, the units of k are:
quiz.explanation: Divide rate units by concentration to the one-half power. Fractional empirical order is allowed and is not fractional molecularity.

quiz.question: For 2N2O5 → 4NO2 + O2, N2O5 disappears at 0.0040 M/s. The normalized reaction rate is:
quiz.explanation: Divide the disappearance rate by the coefficient two; NO2 appears at 0.0080 M/s.

quiz.question: For −d[A]/dt = k[A][B], k = 0.020 L/(mol s) and maintained [B] = 0.50 M. kobs is:
quiz.explanation: Multiply k by the nearly constant B concentration; the units reduce to inverse seconds.

quiz.question: A first-order plot of ln([A]/[A]0) versus time has slope −0.030 min⁻¹. Its half-life is approximately:
quiz.explanation: The positive rate constant is 0.030 min⁻¹ and t_half = ln(2)/k ≈ 23.1 min.

quiz.question: For a 10.0 min first-order half-life, 99.9% completion takes approximately:
quiz.explanation: The fraction remaining is 0.001, so t = 10 ln(1000)/ln(2) ≈ 99.7 min.

quiz.question: Using pseudo-first-order kinetics requires the excess reactant concentration to:
options: Be absent from the original rate law
quiz.explanation: Its concentration is incorporated into kobs only while it changes negligibly.

quiz.explanation: Ea is minus slope times R; convert 49884 J/mol to kJ/mol.

quiz.explanation: The controlled rate ratio gives 4^m=2; taking logarithms gives experimental order m=1/2.
